# Joint Minkowski concavity of the centered projective volume energy

This is an ordinary convex-geometric theorem in every dimension d>=1.
the contributor supplied the direct escort/Hölder proof below; Defect independently
derived the same result through the entropy representation in Section6
and supplied the conditional-map substitution details. No lattice is
transformed, and no OC conclusion is asserted.

For a convex body K in R^d and y in int K define

    E_K(y)=min_a integral_K [1+a.(x-y)]^(-d-1) dx,        (1)

where a ranges over vectors whose displayed denominator is strictly
positive on all of K. The minimum is attained and positive.

**Theorem.** Let K_1,...,K_m be convex bodies in R^d, y_i in int K_i,
and lambda_i>=0 with sum lambda_i=1. Write

    K=sum_i lambda_i K_i,   y=sum_i lambda_i y_i.

Then

    E_K(y)^(1/d) >= sum_i lambda_i E_(K_i)(y_i)^(1/d).    (2)

In particular y -> E_K(y)^(1/d) is concave on int K. The joint statement
allows arbitrary different shapes and arbitrary interior marked points.
It does not assume that the marked points are ordinary centroids.

## 1. Attainment and the exact escort identities

Translate y to zero. The admissible parameter set

    Omega={a:1+a.x>0 for all x in K}

is nonempty, open, convex, and bounded: if r times the unit ball is
contained in K then |a|<1/r. For V(a)=integral_K(1+a.x)^(-d-1),

    grad V=-(d+1) integral_K x(1+a.x)^(-d-2),
    Hess V[b,b]=(d+1)(d+2)
           integral_K (b.x)^2(1+a.x)^(-d-3)>0 for b!=0. (3)

Differentiation is justified locally by the positive compact denominator
bound. To verify coercivity, let a_k approach the boundary of Omega and
choose x_0 in K with1+a_0.x_0=0. Put delta_k=1+a_k.x_0 ->0. A fixed
small (d-1)-disk E centered at0 in a_0-perp lies in the inner ball.
The cone conv(x_0,E) lies in K. Its parameterization
(1-t)x_0+t u has Jacobian c t^(d-1), c>0. Boundedness of a_k gives
1+a_k.x<=delta_k+C t on this cone. Restricting delta_k<=t<=2delta_k
therefore gives V(a_k)>=c'/delta_k ->infinity. For d=1 use E={0}
and counting measure; the same calculation applies. Thus V attains
its unique minimum in Omega.

Restore y, let a be that minimizer, and put

    L(x)=1+a.(x-y),   E=E_K(y).

Stationarity and L=1+a.(x-y) give THREE exact identities:

    integral_K (x-y)L^(-d-2)=0,
    integral_K L^(-d-2)=integral_K L^(-d-1)=E,
    integral_K L*L^(-d-2)=E.                             (4)

Consequently the density

    rho(x)=L(x)^(-d-2)/E on K                             (5)

is a probability density, its barycenter is y, and its expectation of
L is1. The density is continuous and bounded above and strictly away
from zero on K. It extends smoothly to a neighborhood of K.

The map T_a(x-y)=(x-y)/L(x) has Jacobian L^(-d-1), so (1) is exactly
the minimum volume of a projective image of K-y. The proof below uses
only the ordinary integral and escort identities, not any projective
operation on a mixed-integer family.

## 2. Conditional triangular maps with merely convex supports

We record the substitution fact needed for the escort densities. Let
rho be a positive continuous probability density on a convex body K,
with a continuous positive extension to a neighborhood of K. For each
j, let M_j(s) be its marginal density in the first j coordinates,
integrating over the remaining fiber, and put M_0=1.

On the interior of the j-coordinate projection, M_j is positive and
continuous. Here is the continuity justification. An interior point of
a full-dimensional slice, over an interior projected prefix, is an
interior point of K: otherwise a supporting normal must vanish on the
slice direction and would support the projection at its interior point.
Therefore indicators of the fibers converge almost everywhere when
the prefix varies; the only exceptions are on the boundary of the
limiting convex slice, which has zero volume. A fixed bounding box and
the continuous bounded density give dominated convergence. Positivity
comes from the full-dimensional slice. At j=d the assertion is simply
continuity of rho on int K.

For a fixed preceding prefix s, the next-coordinate conditional density
is

    M_j(s,t)/M_(j-1)(s)

on the open projection interval. It is continuous and strictly positive
there. Its cumulative distribution rises continuously and strictly
from0 to1. Invert it at u_j in(0,1), then repeat recursively. This gives
a triangular map X:(0,1)^d -> int K. It is continuous, and for fixed
u_1,...,u_(j-1) its j-th component is differentiable in u_j, with

    a_j(u)=partial X_j/partial u_j
           =M_(j-1)(X_<j)/M_j(X_<=j)>0.                  (6)

Continuity of the inverse follows directly from strict monotonicity:
two interior test points bounding its value continue to bound nearby
values. The conditional projection endpoints are continuous functions
of the preceding interior prefix because they are finite convex or
concave functions on the interior of a convex projection. Thus the
recursive image intervals and their endpoints vary continuously.

Repeated one-dimensional conditional substitution shows that X pushes
uniform cube measure to rho(x)dx. The diagonal products telescope:

    J_X(u):=product_(j=1)^d a_j(u)=1/rho(X(u)).            (7)

No derivatives in preceding-coordinate directions are needed.

Now take finitely many such maps X_i, omit zero lambda_i, and define
S(u)=sum_i lambda_i X_i(u). This is also continuous and triangular,
strictly increasing in its current coordinate, with positive diagonal
derivatives a_j^S=sum_i lambda_i a_ij. Its image U is open and its
inverse is recursively continuous: first invert the first coordinate,
then the second on its continuously varying open interval, and so on.
Thus S is one-to-one. Repeated one-dimensional substitution, starting
with the last coordinate, gives for every nonnegative Borel function G

    integral_U G(x) dx
       =integral_(0,1)^d G(S(u)) product_j a_j^S(u) du.   (8)

Tonelli handles nonnegative functions; no global smoothness of S or
formal off-diagonal determinant is assumed. The image U lies in the
Minkowski sum of the supports, but need not fill it.

Finally generalized Hölder for a finite sum gives

    product_j(sum_i lambda_i a_ij)
       >=[sum_i lambda_i(product_j a_ij)^(1/d)]^d.        (9)

To see this, apply Hölder with d equal exponents to the d arrays
(lambda_i a_ij)^(1/d), then raise to the d-th power. For d=1 it is
an equality. Equations(6)--(9) are the precise triangular transport
facts used below for arbitrary convex bodies.

## 3. Proof of the joint inequality

For each input use its attained denominator L_i, energy E_i, and escort
density rho_i=L_i^(-d-2)/E_i. Let X_i be the maps of Section2, all on
the SAME uniform cube, and set

    S=sum_i lambda_i X_i,
    A=sum_i lambda_i E_i^(1/d)>0,
    w_i=lambda_i E_i^(1/d)/A,
    Lbar(u)=sum_i w_i L_i(X_i(u)).                        (10)

From(4)--(5), the cube expectations satisfy

    E_cube S=y,   E_cube Lbar=1.                         (11)

The diagonal product formula and(9) give

    J_S >=[sum_i lambda_i E_i^(1/d)
                       L_i(X_i)^((d+2)/d)]^d
         >=A^d Lbar^(d+2).                              (12)

The last step is Jensen for the scalar power(d+2)/d>1 with weights w_i.

Take ANY admissible target parameter a for (K,y), and write

    B(u)=1+a.(S(u)-y)>0.

Only this combined denominator is required to be positive. There is
no requirement that individually displaced target denominators be
positive on separate input bodies. By(11), E_cube B=1. Since U=S(cube)
is contained in K, substitution(8) and(12) imply

    integral_K [1+a.(x-y)]^(-d-1) dx
       >= A^d integral_cube Lbar^(d+2)/B^(d+1) du.        (13)

Hölder with exponents d+2 and(d+2)/(d+1) gives

    1=integral Lbar
      <=[integral Lbar^(d+2)/B^(d+1)]^(1/(d+2))
          [integral B]^((d+1)/(d+2)).                    (14)

The last factor is1, so the integral in(13) is at least1. Taking the
infimum over the admissible target parameter proves E_K(y)>=A^d,
which is(2). All densities, maps and integrals used here are actual;
no approximation by sampled fibers or unproved localization principle
is involved.

## 4. Monotonicity, affine scaling, and actual fiber concavity

If K subset L and y in int K, then E_K(y)<=E_L(y): every parameter
admissible for L is admissible for K, and its L integral is at least
its K integral, which in turn is at least E_K(y). This also checks the
direction of the infimum when the parameter domains differ.

For an invertible affine map x -> Qx+b,

    E_(QK+b)(Qy+b)=|det Q| E_K(y).                       (15)

This follows by the change of parameter a -> Q^T a and change of
variables in(1). Thus homothetic pointed copies
K_i=c_i K_0+b_i, y_i=c_i y_0+b_i, c_i>0, attain equality in(2).
The constant in that theorem is exact.

Let C be any compact ordinary convex set whose relevant d-dimensional
fibers C_z are convex bodies. On the convex domain of pairs(z,y) for which
y is interior to such a fiber, define

    F_C(z,y)=E_(C_z)(y)^(1/d).                            (16)

That domain is convex because Minkowski combinations of small balls
inside input fibers remain inside the intermediate fiber. The actual
inclusion sum lambda_i C_(z_i) subset C_(sum lambda_i z_i), monotonicity,
and(2) show that F_C is jointly concave in its continuous base and fiber
coordinates. In particular it can be restricted to integer bases, but
this does not by itself select a mixed-integer point or pay ambient
halfspaces. No projective transformation of the lattice occurs.

## 5. Centroid input specialization

At the ordinary centroid g_K, the minimizer in(1) is a=0 by(3), so
E_K(g_K)=|K|. Conversely equality E_K(y)=|K| implies that a=0 is the
unique minimizer and hence y=g_K. The energy is therefore at most
ordinary volume and has its unique maximum at the ordinary centroid.

For arbitrary input shapes and their ordinary centroids g_i, (2) gives

    E_(sum lambda_i K_i)(sum lambda_i g_i)
       >=[sum lambda_i |K_i|^(1/d)]^d.                   (17)

The marked midpoint need not equal the centroid of the Minkowski sum.
This is a nontrivial ordinary specialization, not a claim that the
source is a mixed-integer point in any ambient task.

## 6. Equivalent maximum-entropy representation

Put p=(d+1)/(d+2). The same energy has the exact variational form

    E_K(y)=sup{(integral_K rho^p)^(d+2):
                  rho>=0, integral rho=1,
                  integral x rho(x)dx=y}.                (18)

For any such density and any admissible affine denominator L, Hölder
applied to rho^p=(rho L)^p L^(-p) gives

    integral rho^p
       <=[integral rho L]^p [integral L^(-d-1)]^(1/(d+2))
       =[integral L^(-d-1)]^(1/(d+2)).

Taking the power d+2 and then the infimum proves the upper bound in(18).
The escort density(5) has integral rho^p=E^(1/(d+2)) and attains equality.
Thus the supremum is attained. This is an ordinary density with a fixed
barycenter; it is not constrained by rho<=1. Replacing it by such a
constraint would change the energy even for an interval.

The entropy representation offers another proof of(2), using(9) and
the reverse Minkowski inequality for the exponent d/(d+2) in(0,1).
The direct proof(10)--(14) avoids needing that additional named
inequality and keeps every normalization explicit.

## 7. Complete equality classification and strict fixed-body concavity

Assume all the retained lambda_i are positive. Equality in(2) holds
if and only if the marked bodies are positively homothetic:

    K_i-y_i=c_i(K_1-y_1),  c_i>0.                         (19)

Sufficiency is the affine-scaling calculation in Section4. Here is
necessity, including the equality cases in the conditional substitution.
Choose the attained target minimizer a in(13). If E_K(y)=A^d, all the
successive nonnegative differences in(12)--(14) have integral zero.
In particular, for almost every cube point both inequalities in(12)
are equalities. Strict convexity of the scalar power(d+2)/d implies

    L_i(X_i(u))=L_j(X_j(u)) for every i,j, a.e. u.         (20)

For d>=2 equality in generalized Hölder(9) says that, at that cube
point, the positive diagonal vectors(a_i1,...,a_id) are proportional
as i varies. Indeed put s_j=sum_i lambda_i a_ij and
p_ij=lambda_i a_ij/s_j. The proof of(9) is
sum_i(product_j p_ij)^(1/d)<=1. Equality in the arithmetic-geometric
mean inequality separately for each i forces p_ij independent of j.
Thus a_ij/a_lj is independent of j. Taking products and using(7),(20)
identifies the factor:

    a_ij/a_lj=(E_i/E_l)^(1/d), for every j, a.e. u.       (21)

For d=1 the same formula follows directly from(7) and(20), without
an equality condition in the tautological one-dimensional Hölder step.

Now fix ANY unit vector e, perform the entire construction in an
orthonormal frame whose first coordinate is e, and use the preceding
equality argument. The first coordinate of each X_i depends only on
u_1. Fubini applied to(21) shows that its one-dimensional quantile
satisfies, with c_i=(E_i/E_1)^(1/d),

    d X_i,1/du_1=c_i d X_1,1/du_1 a.e. on(0,1).

These quantiles are continuously differentiable on each compact
subinterval of(0,1), because their marginal densities are positive
and continuous. Integration therefore gives X_i,1=c_i X_1,1+b_i(e)
throughout(0,1). The escort barycenters determine
b_i(e)=e.y_i-c_i e.y_1. Their endpoint limits are the projection
endpoints of the actual bodies, since each escort density is positive
on the whole interior. Hence

    h_(K_i-y_i)(e)=c_i h_(K_1-y_1)(e).

This holds for every unit e. Equality of support functions proves(19).
There is no need to identify off-diagonal derivatives or to infer
homothety from one chosen transport frame.

In particular, y -> E_K(y)^(1/d) is STRICTLY concave on int K:
for two distinct marked points of the same body, equality would force
c=1 by volume and then a nonzero translation preserving a bounded
body, which is impossible. This conclusion does not use a smoothness
assumption on K, a covariance bound, or an equality case of Berwald.
It does not assert a quantified concavity modulus or an OC consequence.
